meta.name: Tomita/Fuunji-Style Gyokai-Tonkotsu Tsukemen
meta.total_time: ~2 days (Day 1: noodles + tare, Day 2: broth + assembly)
meta.description: An ultra-concentrated dipping ramen inspired by Tomita (Matsudo) and Fuunji (Shinjuku) — the pinnacle of second-generation tsukemen. Built from 74 sources including Tomita's official site, Fuunji owner interviews, the Ramen Heads documentary, and Ramen_Lord's Tomita clone recipe. Features a double soup method (animal broth + fish dashi), three-mechanism thickness (collagen extraction + blended bone solids + emulsification), temperature-controlled fish extraction, fat wheat noodles served cold (shimeru), and the soup-wari finishing ritual.

change_log.summary: Initial recipe synthesized from 8-agent research across 74 sources (Japanese ramen blogs, Reddit/r/ramen, noodle science manufacturers, restaurant deep dives, food science, YouTube creators)

vessels.name: Pressure Cooker (6L+)
vessels.reuse: Blanch bones -> Phase 1-2 pressure cook -> Phase 3 open boil

equipment: Spice Grinder or Mortar and Pestle
Cornstarch or Potato Starch (for dusting noodles)

ingredients.name: Pork Bones (femur/neck)
ingredients.sourcedFrom: All 8 agents — universal for tonkotsu base; Ramen_Lord, Kaonashi, Men to Choujin, Ramen Cook
ingredients.rationale: Femur and neck bones provide the highest collagen yield for thick tonkotsu. 1.5 kg is the standard batch size across 6+ sources for a pressure cooker method.

ingredients.name: Chicken Feet
ingredients.sourcedFrom: 7/8 agents — Ramen_Lord, Kaonashi, RecipeTin, food science sources
ingredients.rationale: 70% pure collagen — the single most efficient gelatin source. Non-negotiable for proper body. 500g provides backbone collagen without overwhelming pork flavor.

ingredients.name: Chicken Backs
ingredients.sourcedFrom: 7/8 agents — Ramen_Lord, Kaonashi, multiple copycat sources
ingredients.rationale: Secondary animal base that mellows the pork intensity. Added in Phase 2 with the pork belly. 1.5 kg balances the pork bones.

ingredients.name: Pork Belly (skin-on, for broth + chashu)
ingredients.sourcedFrom: 5/8 agents — dual-purpose technique from Ramen_Lord, Kaonashi, Ramen Cook
ingredients.rationale: Skin-on pork belly serves double duty: collagen and fat into the broth during Phase 2, then removed and soaked in chashu marinade. 1 kg yields generous chashu slices for 8 servings.

ingredients.name: Yellow Onion (quartered)
ingredients.sourcedFrom: 4/8 agents — Kaonashi, Men to Choujin, Ramen_Lord
ingredients.rationale: Aromatic added late (final hour of bone cook). One medium onion quartered provides sweetness without making broth cloudy.

ingredients.name: Ginger (coins)
ingredients.sourcedFrom: 5/8 agents — standard aromatic across Japanese broth recipes
ingredients.rationale: 4 coin-sized slices. Added late to prevent bitterness. Provides clean aromatic note that cuts through heavy pork flavor.

ingredients.name: Garlic Cloves
ingredients.sourcedFrom: 5/8 agents — standard aromatic; Ramen_Lord, Kaonashi
ingredients.rationale: About 10 cloves. Added late with other aromatics. Contributes depth and rounds out the animal flavor.

ingredients.name: Kombu (dried kelp)
ingredients.sourcedFrom: 7/8 agents — universal glutamic acid foundation; preferred from Hokkaido
ingredients.rationale: Glutamic acid backbone for umami synergy. Split between tare (cold soak for clean extraction) and dashi (heated steep). Hokkaido rishiri or hidaka preferred.

ingredients.name: Niboshi (dried sardines)
ingredients.sourcedFrom: 8/8 agents — primary fish backbone; Setouchi origin preferred (Tomita official site)
ingredients.rationale: The most assertive dried fish — provides the aggressive sardine punch that defines gyokai-tonkotsu. Used in three ways: cold-soaked in tare for clean umami, steeped in dashi for body, and ground into gyofun for finishing powder.

ingredients.name: Katsuobushi (thick-cut dried bonito)
ingredients.sourcedFrom: 8/8 agents — thick-cut (atsukezuri) specified; Kochi origin for premium
ingredients.rationale: Smoky, clean umami top notes. Must use thick-cut (atsukezuri) for slow extraction in dashi — thin flakes would over-extract and turn bitter. Used across tare, dashi, and gyofun.

ingredients.name: Sababushi (thick-cut dried mackerel)
ingredients.sourcedFrom: 7/8 agents — Ramen_Lord, Japanese sources, YouTube creators
ingredients.rationale: Rich, oily fish depth that complements the leaner katsuobushi. Key differentiator for Tomita-style gyokai. 50g in dashi steep + 24g ground into gyofun blend.

ingredients.name: Dried Flounder Powder (optional)
ingredients.sourcedFrom: 3/8 agents — enhancer role; Sweet Post brand on Amazon
ingredients.rationale: 10% of the gyofun blend. Adds a sweet, delicate fish note that rounds out the more aggressive sardine and mackerel. Optional but recommended.

ingredients.name: Koikuchi Soy Sauce (Yamasa or equivalent)
ingredients.sourcedFrom: 8/8 agents — universal tare base; Yamasa Marudaizu recommended for whole-soybean depth
ingredients.rationale: The backbone of all three marinades. Yamasa whole-soybean soy sauce provides deeper flavor than standard brewed. Tomita uses rare ki-joyu (raw soy) but quality koikuchi is the home approximation.

ingredients.name: Hon-Mirin (Takara or equivalent)
ingredients.sourcedFrom: 8/8 agents — universal sweetness component in tare and marinades
ingredients.rationale: Must be hon-mirin (true mirin with 14% alcohol), not mirin-fu (mirin-like seasoning). The alcohol carries flavor compounds and tenderizes the chashu.

ingredients.name: Sake (cooking grade)
ingredients.sourcedFrom: 5/8 agents — tare alcohol component for flavor depth
ingredients.rationale: Boiled to cook off alcohol before adding to tare. Adds flavor complexity and helps dissolve fat-soluble flavor compounds.

ingredients.name: Brown Sugar
ingredients.sourcedFrom: 5/8 agents — balances fish bitterness in tare; sweetens chashu marinade
ingredients.rationale: Molasses notes in brown sugar complement the deep fish flavors better than white sugar. Split between tare and chashu marinade.

ingredients.name: MSG (optional)
ingredients.sourcedFrom: 4/8 agents — umami booster; standard in professional ramen
ingredients.rationale: Optional but standard in professional ramen kitchens. Amplifies the glutamic acid from kombu and soy sauce. Omit if preferred.

ingredients.name: Bread Flour (King Arthur, 12.7% protein)
ingredients.sourcedFrom: Ramen_Lord Tomita clone — highest confidence noodle formula; Yamato Noodle science
ingredients.rationale: High-protein bread flour (12.7%) provides the strong gluten network needed for thick, chewy tsukemen noodles. 94% of the flour blend.

ingredients.name: Whole Wheat Flour
ingredients.sourcedFrom: Ramen_Lord Tomita clone — 6% whole wheat for color and flavor
ingredients.rationale: 6% whole wheat provides the golden-brown color, earthy wheat aroma, and mineral specks characteristic of Tomita's noodles. Slightly reduces gluten for a more tender bite.

ingredients.name: Water (for noodle dough)
ingredients.sourcedFrom: Ramen_Lord Tomita clone — 42% hydration, confirmed sweet spot for tsukemen
ingredients.rationale: 42% hydration is the consensus sweet spot for thick tsukemen noodles (range: 38-45%). Higher hydration makes sheeting easier but produces softer noodles.

ingredients.name: Kansui (80% Na2CO3, 20% K2CO3)
ingredients.sourcedFrom: Ramen_Lord Tomita clone — reversed ratio confirmed by Yamato Noodle, Myojo USA
ingredients.rationale: Reversed 80:20 Na:K ratio (opposite of standard ramen's 20:80). Sodium carbonate dominant = softer, more supple texture appropriate for thick noodles. 1% baker's percentage.

ingredients.name: Salt (for noodle dough)
ingredients.sourcedFrom: Ramen_Lord Tomita clone — 1% baker's percentage
ingredients.rationale: Strengthens the gluten network and adds flavor to the noodles. Dissolved with kansui in the water before mixing.

ingredients.name: Eggs (for ajitama)
ingredients.sourcedFrom: Universal — standard ramen topping; 6 large eggs ~60g each
ingredients.rationale: 6 large eggs for 8 servings (allows for breakage). Soft-boiled to jammy center, marinated in soy-mirin solution.

ingredients.name: Water (for ajitama marinade)
ingredients.sourcedFrom: Standard ajitama technique — dilutes marinade to prevent over-seasoning
ingredients.rationale: Dilutes the soy-mirin marinade so eggs absorb flavor gently over 4-12 hours without becoming overly salty.

ingredients.name: Water (for chashu marinade)
ingredients.sourcedFrom: Synthesis Component 5 — standard chashu braising liquid ratio
ingredients.rationale: Dilutes the soy-mirin-sugar chashu soak so the pork belly absorbs flavor evenly. The belly is already cooked from the broth phase.

ingredients.name: Water (for broth)
ingredients.sourcedFrom: Ramen_Lord, Kaonashi — standard bone:water ratio ~1:1 (kg:L)
ingredients.rationale: Starting water for the pressure cooker. Will reduce significantly during cooking. Target final volume ~3L after blending solids back in. 4L starting water with ~3.5 kg bones/meat.

ingredients.name: Water (for fish dashi)
ingredients.sourcedFrom: Synthesis master recipe — fish dashi extraction base
ingredients.rationale: Water for steeping kombu, niboshi, katsuobushi, and sababushi. Heated to 176°F (80°C), never boiled. Yields ~1.2L after straining and pressing.

ingredients.name: Rice Vinegar (unseasoned)
ingredients.sourcedFrom: 7/8 agents — Ramen_Lord, Kaonashi, Ramen Database, food science
ingredients.rationale: The acid that prevents palate fatigue. A small splash per bowl brightens the ultra-rich dipping broth. Without it, the richness becomes cloying. Marukan Genuine Brewed recommended.

ingredients.name: Nori Sheets
ingredients.sourcedFrom: Universal topping — 2 half-sheets per serving, ~3g total per serving
ingredients.rationale: Standard tsukemen garnish. 16 half-sheets (2 per bowl). Placed upright in the dipping broth so they soften gradually.

ingredients.name: Menma (seasoned bamboo shoots)
ingredients.sourcedFrom: Universal topping — standard ramen garnish
ingredients.rationale: About 15g per bowl. Provides crunch and a mild sweetness that contrasts with the intense broth. Use jarred/packaged menma.

ingredients.name: Green Onions (sliced thin)
ingredients.sourcedFrom: Universal topping — standard ramen garnish
ingredients.rationale: Fresh, sharp contrast to the rich broth. Sliced thin on the bias. Some reserved for soup-wari finishing.

states.title: Prepare Workspace
states.direction: Gather all vessels, equipment, and ingredients. Weigh out all ingredients. Separate multi-use ingredients into labeled containers: soy sauce (450g tare, 200g chashu, 50g ajitama), mirin (50g tare, 100g chashu, 50g ajitama), kombu (15g tare, 20g dashi), niboshi (20g tare, 80g dashi, 12g gyofun), katsuobushi (15g tare, 50g dashi, 18g gyofun), sababushi (50g dashi, 24g gyofun), brown sugar (20g tare, 50g chashu). Remove niboshi heads and guts from larger sardines.
states.exit_condition: All ingredients weighed, separated into labeled containers by sub-recipe, niboshi cleaned, workspace organized

notes.text: Separating multi-use ingredients now prevents mistakes later — soy sauce, mirin, kombu, niboshi, katsuobushi, sababushi, and brown sugar all appear in multiple sub-recipes
Remove niboshi heads and guts by pinching — larger sardines carry bitterness from digestive organs. This is the #6 most common mistake.
This recipe spans 2 days. Day 1: tare cold soak + noodle making. Day 2: broth + dashi + assembly. Plan accordingly.

states.title: Cold Soak Tare
states.direction: Combine 450g soy sauce, 50g mirin, 15g kombu, and 20g niboshi in medium saucepan (V3). Stir gently to combine. Cover and refrigerate for 6-24 hours.
states.exit_condition: Kombu and niboshi have soaked in soy-mirin mixture for minimum 6 hours, liquid has darkened slightly

notes.text: Overnight cold soak develops dramatically cleaner umami vs hot extraction — don't skip this
Start this the evening of Day 1, along with the noodles. Both need overnight rest.
The kombu will have expanded significantly and the liquid will be noticeably more viscous from extracted glutamic acid

states.title: Heat Tare
states.direction: Boil 20g sake in a separate small vessel for 5 minutes to cook off alcohol. Add sake to the cold-soaked tare mixture in V3. Place V3 on stove over medium-low heat. Slowly bring to 175°F (79°C) — do NOT let it boil. Hold at 175°F (79°C) for 15 minutes. Remove and discard the kombu.
states.exit_condition: Tare held at 175°F (79°C) for 15 minutes, kombu removed, liquid is fragrant and slightly thickened

notes.text: Boiling the tare would destroy the clean umami built during the cold soak — use a thermometer
The niboshi stay in — they continue to add depth. Only the kombu is removed to prevent sliminess.

states.title: Finish Tare
states.direction: Add 20g brown sugar, 15g katsuobushi, and 5g MSG (optional) to the heated tare in V3. Stir to dissolve sugar. Remove from heat. Steep for 15 minutes. Strain through fine-mesh strainer, pressing katsuobushi to extract all liquid. Transfer to a jar or container. Refrigerate. Keeps for months.
states.exit_condition: Tare strained, dark and aromatic, transferred to container for storage

notes.text: The brown sugar balances the bitterness from the dried fish — taste and adjust if needed
Press the katsuobushi firmly in the strainer — significant flavor remains in the solids
Finished tare should taste very concentrated and salty. It will be diluted by the broth at assembly.

states.title: Dissolve Kansui and Salt
states.direction: In a measuring cup or small bowl, combine 420g water with 10g kansui powder and 10g salt. Stir vigorously until completely dissolved. The water will turn slightly yellow from the kansui.
states.exit_condition: Kansui and salt fully dissolved, water is slightly yellow, no visible granules

notes.text: If using baked baking soda instead of commercial kansui: bake baking soda at 250°F (121°C) for 1 hour, then use 10g of the result as pure sodium carbonate
The 80:20 Na:K ratio is reversed from standard ramen (which is 20:80). Sodium-heavy = softer, more supple thick noodles.

states.title: Mix Noodle Dough
states.direction: Combine 940g bread flour and 60g whole wheat flour in a large bowl or stand mixer with paddle attachment. With the mixer on low speed, slowly stream in the kansui water over 3-4 minutes. Mix until the flour is evenly hydrated and forms shaggy, crumbly pieces. Do not overmix — the dough will not form a ball at this stage.
states.exit_condition: Flour evenly hydrated, forms crumbly clumps when squeezed — no dry pockets, no smooth dough ball

notes.text: At 42% hydration this dough is very stiff. It will look too dry — this is normal. The rest period does the work of bringing it together.
Stream the water in slowly. Adding too fast creates wet pockets surrounded by dry flour.

states.title: Rest Dough (First Rest)
states.direction: Gather the crumbly dough into a rough mass. Wrap tightly in plastic wrap. Rest at room temperature for 30-60 minutes. The gluten will relax and the moisture will equalize throughout the dough.
states.exit_condition: Dough has rested 30-60 minutes, feels slightly more pliable when pressed through the plastic

notes.text: This rest is critical — the moisture migrates into dry pockets and the gluten begins to develop without mechanical work

states.title: Sheet Noodles (Lamination)
states.direction: Unwrap dough. Pass through pasta machine on the widest setting. The dough will be rough and may crumble — this is normal. Fold the sheet in thirds (like a letter). Rotate 90 degrees. Pass through widest setting again. Repeat this fold-and-roll process 5-8 times until the dough sheet is smooth, elastic, and has a consistent texture.
states.exit_condition: Dough sheet is smooth, elastic, and passes through the widest setting without tearing or crumbling

notes.text: This lamination process builds the gluten network that gives tsukemen noodles their signature chew. 5-8 passes minimum.
Dust with cornstarch or potato starch as needed to prevent sticking. Do not use flour — it changes the ratio.
If the dough resists rolling, cover and rest 5 minutes before continuing. Fighting tight gluten tears the sheet.

states.title: Rest Dough (Second Rest)
states.direction: Wrap the laminated dough sheet in plastic wrap. Rest at room temperature for 30 minutes. This relaxes the gluten before final rolling.
states.exit_condition: Dough has rested 30 minutes, gluten is relaxed and sheet is more pliable

notes.text: Yamato Noodle (noodle machine manufacturer) recommends multiple rest periods for best texture development

states.title: Roll to Final Thickness
states.direction: Pass the rested dough through progressively thinner settings on the pasta machine, one setting at a time. Never skip settings — this tears the gluten network. Target final thickness: approximately 3mm (about setting 3-4 on most machines, depending on brand).
states.exit_condition: Dough sheet is uniformly 3mm thick, smooth surface with no tears or thin spots

notes.text: 3mm is thick for pasta but correct for tsukemen. These are fat, square noodles — do not roll thinner.
If your pasta machine markings don't indicate mm, measure with a ruler. 3mm is about the thickness of two stacked credit cards.

states.title: Cut Noodles
states.direction: Dust the dough sheet generously with cornstarch or potato starch. Cut through the 3mm cutter attachment (or fold the sheet and cut by hand into 3mm-wide strips). Toss cut noodles in more starch to prevent sticking. Portion into 200g bundles. Place each portion in a ziplock bag, pressing out air.
states.exit_condition: Noodles cut to 3mm width, portioned into 200g bundles, each bagged separately with starch dusting

notes.text: 200g per serving is larger than standard ramen (100-150g). Tsukemen noodles are the star, not a supporting actor.
Expect approximately 7 portions from 1000g flour + 420g water (total dough ~1440g, minus some waste from trimming).
Industry equivalent: #12 cutter number (Myojo USA standard for tsukemen)

states.title: Age Noodles (24h Minimum)
states.direction: Refrigerate the bagged noodle portions for a minimum of 24 hours. 48-72 hours produces even better results. The aging eliminates air bubbles, develops flavor, and mellows the alkaline taste from the kansui.
states.exit_condition: Noodles have rested in refrigerator for minimum 24 hours

notes.text: 24-hour noodle rest is a strong consensus across sources. Fresh noodles without resting have an unpleasant alkaline bite and inferior texture.
If testing: compare noodles at 24, 48, and 72 hours. Most sources agree 48h is the sweet spot for flavor development.

states.title: Blanch Bones
states.direction: Place 1500g pork bones and 500g chicken feet in pressure cooker (V1). Cover with cold water. Bring to a rolling boil over high heat. Boil for 10 minutes — the water will turn grey and scummy. This removes impurities, blood, and off-flavors.
states.exit_condition: Water is grey and scummy, bones have been at a rolling boil for 10 minutes

notes.text: This blanching step is non-negotiable — it removes the 'off' flavors that would make the final broth taste muddy instead of clean and rich
The amount of scum is normal and expected. Some bones produce more than others depending on freshness.

states.title: Clean Bones and Pot
states.direction: Drain and discard the blanching water. Rinse each bone under running water, scrubbing off any remaining dark matter, coagulated blood, or scum. Thoroughly clean the pressure cooker (V1). Return cleaned bones and chicken feet to the clean pot.
states.exit_condition: All bones are clean (no dark spots or scum), pot is clean, bones returned to pot

notes.text: Scrub the bones individually — any remaining blood or scum will make the broth taste funky even after hours of cooking
Clean the pot thoroughly as well — residual scum on the pot walls will dissolve back into the fresh broth

states.title: Pressure Cook Phase 1 (Bone Extraction)
states.direction: Add 4000g water to the cleaned bones in pressure cooker (V1). Lock lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 1 hour. The bones will begin to break down and release collagen into the broth.
states.exit_condition: 1 hour at high pressure complete, broth is starting to turn milky white

notes.text: Pressure cooking accelerates collagen extraction by 3-4x. This 1-hour phase at pressure equals 3-4 hours of open-pot boiling.
The broth will already look different from typical stock — cloudier, thicker. This is the collagen emulsifying.

states.title: Pressure Cook Phase 2 (Collagen Build)
states.direction: Release pressure carefully. Open lid. Add 1500g chicken backs and 1000g pork belly (rolled and tied with kitchen twine for easy removal). Lock lid. Return to high pressure for 1 additional hour.
states.exit_condition: 1 hour at high pressure complete, broth is opaque and creamy white, pork belly is tender

notes.text: Tie the pork belly with kitchen twine so you can remove it in one piece for chashu. It will be very tender after this phase.
The chicken backs add a different collagen profile that makes the broth silkier. The pork belly skin is a collagen bomb.

states.title: Remove Pork Belly for Chashu
states.direction: Release pressure. Carefully remove the rolled pork belly from the broth using tongs. It will be very tender — handle gently to keep it intact. Set aside to cool slightly before transferring to the chashu marinade (see MARINATE_CHASHU). Leave all other bones and meat in the pot.
states.exit_condition: Pork belly removed intact, set aside for chashu marinade

notes.text: The pork belly has served its dual purpose: collagen and fat into the broth, now it becomes your chashu topping
If the belly falls apart, that is fine — it was well-cooked. The chashu will still be delicious, just harder to slice neatly.

states.title: Add Aromatics (Final Hour)
states.direction: With the lid off, bring the broth in V1 to an open boil over medium-high heat. Add 200g quartered onion, 20g ginger coins, and 50g garlic cloves. Boil uncovered for 1 hour, stirring occasionally. The broth will reduce and concentrate.
states.exit_condition: Broth has boiled uncovered for 1 hour, aromatics are soft, liquid has reduced and is thick and opaque

notes.text: Aromatics are added late deliberately — early addition during pressure cooking makes them bitter. 45-60 minutes is the consensus window.
Open boiling serves two purposes: reduction (concentrates flavor) and emulsification (violent boiling mechanically emulsifies fat into the gelatin-rich broth).

states.title: Strain Broth (Keep the Solids!)
states.direction: Set a colander over a large pot or bowl. Pour the broth through the colander, catching all the liquid. DO NOT discard the solids. Set the strained broth aside. Pick out and discard only the largest intact bones. Keep all the soft, broken-down meat, cartilage, vegetables, and small bone fragments for the next step.
states.exit_condition: Broth strained and set aside, solids separated — large intact bones discarded, soft material retained for blending

notes.text: This is NOT a normal straining step. You are keeping the solids — they become the slurry that makes the broth tsukemen-thick.
Use a colander (large holes), not a fine-mesh strainer. You want to catch only the big bones, not filter out the good stuff.

states.title: Blend Bone Slurry (The Secret Technique)
states.direction: Transfer approximately 2/3 of the retained cooked solids (soft bones, meat, cartilage, vegetables) to the blender (V4) with enough strained broth to blend smoothly. Blend on high until completely smooth — a thick, creamy slurry with no chunks. Return the slurry to the strained broth. Stir to combine. If using an immersion blender, add the solids directly to the broth pot and blend in place. Adjust total volume to approximately 3L by adding water if needed or reducing further if too thin.
states.exit_condition: Slurry blended smooth and reincorporated into broth, total volume approximately 3L, broth is thick, opaque, and coats the back of a spoon

notes.text: This is THE signature technique for Tomita-level thickness — without blending solids back in, you get regular tonkotsu, not tsukemen-thick
The target consistency is 'gravy-thick' — it should coat a spoon and drip slowly, not run off. If too thin, reduce on the stove. If too thick, add water.
For even more emulsification, hit the final broth with an immersion blender for 30 seconds (forced emulsification technique from Ramen Cook).

states.title: Heat Dashi Water
states.direction: In the large pot (V2), heat 1500g water over medium heat. Monitor with a thermometer. Bring to exactly 176°F (80°C). Do not let it boil.
states.exit_condition: Water is at 176°F (80°C), stable, not boiling

notes.text: A thermometer is essential here. The difference between 176°F (80°C) and 212°F (100°C) is the difference between clean umami and bitter fish soup.

states.title: Steep Kombu and Niboshi
states.direction: Add 20g kombu and 80g niboshi to the 176°F (80°C) water in V2. Maintain temperature at 176°F (80°C) for 20 minutes. Adjust burner as needed to hold temperature. Do NOT let it boil.
states.exit_condition: Kombu and niboshi have steeped at 176°F (80°C) for 20 minutes, liquid is golden and aromatic

notes.text: Boiling fish is the #1 mistake — it extracts bitter compounds. Steep at 176-194°F (80-90°C) only
The kombu should be soft and expanded. The niboshi should be soft but not disintegrating.

states.title: Add Katsuobushi and Sababushi
states.direction: Remove kombu from V2 and discard. Add 50g thick-cut katsuobushi and 50g thick-cut sababushi to the pot. Stir gently to submerge. Immediately turn off the heat.
states.exit_condition: Katsuobushi and sababushi added, heat turned off, flakes are submerged in the liquid

notes.text: Thick-cut (atsukezuri) is essential — thin flakes would over-extract in the steep time and turn bitter
Remove the kombu before adding the bonito/mackerel to prevent sliminess from over-extracted kombu

states.title: Steep Fish Off Heat
states.direction: Let the katsuobushi and sababushi steep in the hot liquid off heat for 15 minutes. Do not stir — let them settle naturally.
states.exit_condition: Fish flakes have steeped for 15 minutes, liquid is dark golden and intensely fragrant

notes.text: The residual heat (around 158-176°F / 70-80°C) is perfect for extracting inosinic acid from the dried fish without bitter compounds

states.title: Strain Dashi
states.direction: Strain the fish dashi through a fine-mesh strainer lined with cheesecloth or a clean kitchen towel. Press the fish solids firmly to extract all liquid. Discard the spent fish. Reserve the strained dashi.
states.exit_condition: Dashi is clear golden, strained through fine mesh, fish solids pressed dry and discarded

notes.text: Press firmly — significant flavor remains in the solids. You should extract at least 1-1.2L of concentrated dashi from the 1.5L starting water.
Reserve some of this dashi for the soup-wari dilution broth. Set aside about 500ml separately.

states.title: Add Gyofun to Broth
states.direction: Add 30g gyofun (fish powder, from the GYOFUN stage) to the animal broth. Stir to incorporate. Then add the strained fish dashi (minus the 500ml reserved for soup-wari). Stir to combine the double soup. Bring to a gentle simmer to meld the flavors for 5 minutes. Taste and adjust seasoning.
states.exit_condition: Double soup combined — animal broth + fish dashi + gyofun — simmered 5 minutes, thick and intensely aromatic

notes.text: This is the double soup merger — the defining moment where animal richness meets fish complexity. The umami synergy between glutamic acid (kombu, soy) and inosinic acid (fish) amplifies perceived umami by approximately 8x.
The broth should be thick enough to coat noodles when dipping but remember it will be further concentrated by the tare at assembly.

states.title: Toast Fish for Gyofun
states.direction: In a dry pan over medium-low heat, lightly toast the gyofun fish components separately: 24g sababushi flakes, 18g katsuobushi flakes, and 12g niboshi. Toast each for 1-2 minutes until fragrant and slightly darkened. Do not burn. Transfer to a plate to cool.
states.exit_condition: All fish components toasted until fragrant, slightly darkened, cooled on a plate

notes.text: Toasting before grinding deepens the flavor and makes the fish more brittle for easier grinding
Toast each component separately — they have different moisture levels and burn at different rates

states.title: Grind Gyofun Blend
states.direction: Combine the toasted fish components with 6g dried flounder powder (if using) in a spice grinder or mortar and pestle. Grind to a fine powder. The final blend ratio is 40% sababushi, 30% katsuobushi, 20% niboshi, 10% flounder. Store in an airtight container. Total yield: approximately 60g. 30g goes into the broth; remaining 30g is for per-bowl garnish.
states.exit_condition: Gyofun ground to fine powder, stored in airtight container, divided: 30g for broth, 30g for garnish

notes.text: This is the signature Fuunji/Tomita finishing powder. The mound of gyofun on top of the dipping broth progressively intensifies as you eat — it sinks to the bottom and concentrates the final bites.
Fuunji uses pure bonito powder; this blend is closer to Tomita's mixed-fish approach. Experiment with ratios.

states.title: Marinate Chashu
states.direction: In the small pan (V6), combine 200g soy sauce, 200g water, 100g mirin, and 50g brown sugar. Stir over low heat until sugar dissolves. Let cool slightly. Place the reserved cooked pork belly in a container or ziplock bag. Pour the marinade over the pork belly. Refrigerate for at least 2 hours, up to overnight. Turn the pork occasionally for even absorption.
states.exit_condition: Pork belly submerged in marinade, refrigerated for minimum 2 hours, darkened in color

notes.text: The pork belly is already fully cooked from the broth phase — this marinade is purely for flavoring, not cooking
Save the used chashu marinade — it can be added to the ajitama marinade or used to season future dishes. Known as 'chashu dare' in ramen shops.

states.title: Soft-Boil Eggs
states.direction: Bring a pot of water to a rolling boil. Gently lower 6 eggs into the water. Boil for exactly 6.5 minutes for a jammy, just-set yolk. Immediately transfer to an ice bath. Peel after 10 minutes in the ice bath.
states.exit_condition: Eggs boiled 6.5 minutes, ice-bathed, peeled — yolks are jammy and just set, not runny or hard

notes.text: 6.5 minutes from a rolling boil produces the ideal ajitama yolk — jammy in the center with a thin set outer ring. Adjust by 15-30 seconds depending on altitude and egg size.
Peel under gently running water for cleanest results. Older eggs (7+ days) peel much easier than fresh ones.

states.title: Marinate Ajitama
states.direction: Combine 50g soy sauce, 50g mirin, and 100g water in a container or ziplock bag. Add the peeled soft-boiled eggs. Ensure eggs are fully submerged. Refrigerate for 4-12 hours, turning occasionally.
states.exit_condition: Eggs have marinated minimum 4 hours, whites are golden brown, flavor has penetrated

notes.text: 4 hours gives light flavor and color. 8-12 hours gives deeper penetration. Beyond 12 hours the whites can become rubbery.
A ziplock bag uses less marinade than a container since you can press out the air to surround the eggs

states.title: Heat Dipping Bowls
states.direction: Fill each dipping bowl with boiling water and let stand for 2-3 minutes to pre-heat. Pour out the water just before assembling. The bowl must be scorching hot because the noodles are served cold.
states.exit_condition: All dipping bowls are heated through, water poured out, ready for broth assembly

notes.text: This is critical for tsukemen — the noodles are cold and will rapidly cool the dipping broth. Starting with a hot bowl extends the window of optimal temperature.

states.title: Assemble Dipping Broth
states.direction: In each pre-heated dipping bowl: add 30ml tare (about 2 tablespoons). Ladle in 200ml of the combined broth (reheated to near-boiling). Stir to dissolve tare into broth. Add a splash of rice vinegar (about 1.2g / 1/4 teaspoon). Mound 3-4g gyofun (about 1 teaspoon) on top of the broth — do not stir it in.
states.exit_condition: Each dipping bowl has tare, hot broth, vinegar, and a mound of gyofun on top — broth is near-boiling

notes.text: The gyofun sits on top as a mound — it progressively dissolves as you dip noodles, intensifying the broth over the course of the meal. This is the Fuunji signature.
Rice vinegar is essential — it prevents palate fatigue with this level of richness. Without it, the broth becomes cloying after a few bites.
Reheat the broth to near-boiling before ladling — it must be scorching to compensate for the cold noodles

states.title: Cook Noodles
states.direction: Bring a large pot of water to a vigorous rolling boil. Cook one portion (200g) of aged noodles for 7 minutes at a full boil. Do not crowd the pot — cook 1-2 portions at a time maximum. The noodles should be al dente with a slight chew in the center.
states.exit_condition: Noodles cooked 7 minutes at full boil, al dente with slight chew in center, no raw flour taste

notes.text: 7 minutes is for 3mm homemade noodles. If using store-bought Sun Noodle Kaedama, follow their package instructions (usually 2-3 minutes).
Use a lot of water — at least 2L per portion. Crowding drops the temperature and makes noodles gummy.

states.title: Cold Shock Noodles (Shimeru)
states.direction: Drain cooked noodles immediately. Plunge into a bowl of ice-cold water (V5). Massage the noodles under cold running water, rubbing between your hands until completely chilled and all surface starch is removed. The noodles should feel firm, springy, and slightly squeaky. Drain well and arrange on a plate or bamboo mat.
states.exit_condition: Noodles are cold, firm, springy with no residual surface starch

notes.text: This is the shimeru technique — the cold shock tightens the gluten network, creating the signature springy, bouncy texture of tsukemen noodles. Skipping this turns great noodles into a soggy mess.
Massage thoroughly — surface starch makes the noodles slimy and prevents the dipping broth from clinging properly
The contrast between ice-cold noodles and scorching-hot dipping broth is fundamental to the tsukemen experience

states.title: Plate Noodles
states.direction: Arrange the drained, cold noodles on a plate or bamboo mat (zaru). Twist or fold them into a neat mound. The noodles should glisten slightly but not be wet.
states.exit_condition: Noodles arranged neatly on plate, well-drained, glistening but not wet

notes.text: Tsukemen noodle plating is about visual appeal — a neat twist shows off the thick, golden noodles

states.title: Add Toppings
states.direction: Slice the marinated chashu into 1cm-thick rounds (2 slices per serving). Halve the ajitama eggs. On each noodle plate, arrange: 2 slices chashu, half an ajitama egg, a small mound of menma (about 15g), 2 half-sheets of nori, and a scattering of sliced green onion. Place condiments on the side: extra gyofun, yuzu peel or yuzu kosho (if available), and diced raw onion.
states.exit_condition: Each serving has noodle plate with toppings and a dipping bowl with broth — ready to serve

notes.text: Nori can be placed on the noodle plate or stood upright in the dipping broth — both presentations are traditional
Serve immediately — the clock starts ticking as soon as the hot broth meets the bowl. The dipping broth cools with each noodle dip.

states.title: Heat Soup-Wari Broth
states.direction: Heat the reserved 500ml fish dashi (from STRAIN_DASHI step) in a small pot or kettle until steaming hot. Transfer to a serving vessel — a small teapot, gravy boat, or heated carafe. This is the soup-wari dilution broth.
states.exit_condition: Fish dashi is steaming hot and in a serving vessel, ready for diners to pour

notes.text: If you did not reserve enough fish dashi, light chicken broth or even hot water works as a substitute — the remaining dipping sauce is so concentrated it can handle significant dilution.

states.title: Serve Soup-Wari
states.direction: After finishing noodles, provide the hot dilution broth. Each diner pours hot fish dashi into their remaining dipping sauce to dilute to a sippable consistency — approximately 50% dilution. Add yuzu peel, extra green onion, or leftover chashu bits to the diluted soup.
states.exit_condition: Diners have diluted remaining dipping sauce to sippable consistency and enjoyed the soup-wari

notes.text: Soup-wari is the reward for finishing the noodles — the dipping sauce transforms into a rich, balanced soup when diluted
The recipe is designed for this dual-use: concentrated enough to coat cold noodles, balanced enough to drink when diluted ~50%. This is why the tare-to-broth ratio matters at assembly.
At Fuunji, soup-wari is offered free of charge — the shop considers it part of the meal, not an extra

research.strategy: 8 parallel search agents using distinct strategies: copycat recipe aggregation, Japanese-language ramen blogs (Men to Choujin, Ramen Cook), food science and collagen extraction research, Reddit/r/ramen community (especially Ramen_Lord's Tomita clone), YouTube creator analysis, noodle science and manufacturing (Yamato Noodle, Myojo), specialty ingredient sourcing, and restaurant/documentary deep dives (Tomita official site, Fuunji owner interview, Ramen Heads documentary). Key insight: the 'secret' is three-mechanism thickness (collagen + blended solids + emulsification) combined with umami synergy between glutamic acid and inosinic acid (~8x amplification).

techniques.name: Double soup method (animal broth + separate fish dashi)
techniques.sourcedFrom: All 8 agents — universal across all tsukemen sources; Tomita, Fuunji, Ramen_Lord, Men to Choujin, Ramen Cook
techniques.rationale: Animal broth needs rolling boil for hours to extract collagen; fish needs gentle steep at 176-194°F (80-90°C) for 15-45 minutes. Boiling fish extracts bitter compounds. Cooking them separately and combining at the end preserves the best qualities of both.

techniques.name: Blending bone solids back into broth (slurry technique)
techniques.sourcedFrom: All 8 agents — Ramen_Lord, Men to Choujin (doro), Ramen Cook, Kaonashi; Tomita's 'gravy-thick' profile requires this
techniques.rationale: THE signature technique for Tomita-level thickness. Blend 2/3 of strained solids into a smooth slurry and return to broth. Without this, you get standard thick tonkotsu — not the gravy-like consistency that defines tsukemen dipping broth.

techniques.name: Temperature-controlled fish extraction at 176-194°F (80-90°C)
techniques.sourcedFrom: All 8 agents — universal consensus; Ramen Chemistry, Myojo USA dashi guide, food science sources
techniques.rationale: Sub-boiling extraction pulls clean inosinic acid (umami) from dried fish without the bitter compounds released above 194°F (90°C). Kombu first (20 min), then katsuobushi/sababushi off heat (15 min). The #1 mistake cited across sources is boiling the fish.

techniques.name: Tare cold soak (kombu + niboshi in soy sauce, 6-24 hours)
techniques.sourcedFrom: 6/8 agents — Ramen Cook, Men to Choujin, Ramen Chemistry; strong consensus on cold vs hot extraction
techniques.rationale: Overnight cold soak in soy sauce extracts glutamic acid from kombu and inosinic acid from niboshi more cleanly than hot extraction. The result is a dramatically cleaner, deeper umami compared to simply simmering the ingredients.

techniques.name: Noodles served cold (shimeru technique)
techniques.sourcedFrom: All 8 agents — universal; defines tsukemen as distinct from ramen
techniques.rationale: Cold water shock after boiling tightens the gluten network, creating springy, bouncy texture and removing surface starch. The temperature contrast with scorching-hot dipping broth is fundamental to the tsukemen experience. Noodle-centric dining.

techniques.name: Soup-wari finishing dilution system
techniques.sourcedFrom: All 8 agents — universal; Wikipedia, Fuunji reviews, Yamachan Ramen 101
techniques.rationale: After finishing noodles, hot dashi dilutes the remaining concentrated dipping sauce into a sippable soup. The recipe must be designed for this dual use: concentrated enough to coat cold noodles, balanced enough to drink when diluted approximately 50%.

techniques.name: Pressure cooking acceleration (5-6h vs 13-18h stovetop)
techniques.sourcedFrom: 6/8 agents — Ramen_Lord pressure cook method, Ramen Cook, food science sources
techniques.rationale: Pressure cooking at 15 PSI raises water temperature to 250°F (121°C), accelerating collagen hydrolysis by 3-4x. A phased approach (bones first, then chicken + pork, then aromatics) optimizes extraction from each component.

techniques.name: Gyofun as finishing garnish (progressive intensification)
techniques.sourcedFrom: 7/8 agents — Fuunji signature, Ramen_Lord, Mutual Trading, CooNelNel guide
techniques.rationale: A mound of fish powder on top of the dipping broth that progressively dissolves as you dip noodles — the broth intensifies with each bite. Fuunji's signature. Also added to the broth base (30g) for foundational fish depth.

techniques.name: 24-hour minimum noodle rest
techniques.sourcedFrom: 6/8 agents — Ramen_Lord, Yamato Noodle, Men to Choujin hydration experiment
techniques.rationale: Refrigerated aging after cutting eliminates air bubbles, develops wheat flavor, and mellows the alkaline taste from kansui. Most sources agree 48h is the sweet spot. Fresh noodles without resting have an unpleasant alkaline bite.

techniques.name: Aromatics added late (final 45-60 minutes only)
techniques.sourcedFrom: 6/8 agents — Ramen_Lord, Kaonashi, Men to Choujin; consistent across pressure cook and stovetop methods
techniques.rationale: Onion, ginger, and garlic added during the final open-boil phase (last 45-60 minutes). Early addition during pressure cooking extracts bitter compounds from alliums. Late addition provides clean aromatic notes.

techniques.name: Forced emulsification via immersion blender
techniques.sourcedFrom: 3/8 agents — Ramen Cook (nyuuka technique), food science sources
techniques.rationale: A hand blender mechanically emulsifies fat into gelatin-rich broth in seconds, shortcutting what 10-20 hours of rolling boil achieves naturally. Optional technique to boost creaminess after combining the double soup.

techniques.name: Reversed kansui ratio 80:20 Na:K for thick noodles
techniques.sourcedFrom: Ramen_Lord Tomita clone, Yamato Noodle kansui science, Myojo USA kansui guide
techniques.rationale: Standard ramen uses 20:80 Na:K (potassium-dominant for firm thin noodles). Tsukemen reverses this to 80:20 (sodium-dominant) because sodium carbonate produces softer, more supple texture appropriate for the extreme thickness of 3mm noodles.
